Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma

The Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma is a living government with a history distinct from the Absentee Shawnee and the Shawnee Tribe. A historical account follows removal from Ohio and institutional change in Oklahoma, while the Tribe’s educational companion and a 2024 participant report describe continuing work to learn and share that history.

Read the sources [1] Oklahoma Historical Society, The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture [2] Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma [3] WYSO, republished by WOSU Public Media

Start reading here

Begin with the Eastern Shawnee government’s educational framing, then compare a dated historical synthesis and a reported educational visit. These selected works offer different perspectives; they do not exhaust the community’s history or stand for all Shawnee governments.

  1. Educator’s Guide: Resilience Through Adversity — A Companion Guide for Educators and Researchers

    Start with the Tribe’s explanation of its historical education project and the selected Identity chapter synopses.

  2. Shawnee, Eastern

    Follow the selected removal and institutional chronology in Pamela A. Smith’s dated historical synthesis, keeping the exclusions in its annotation.

  3. 60 members of the Eastern Shawnee tribe made cross-country journey to Ohio

    Read named participants’ 2024 perspectives on learning and telling Eastern Shawnee history during a return visit to Ohio.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Removal and a distinct institutional history

Pamela A. Smith’s Oklahoma Historical Society account traces an Ohio Shawnee–Seneca association through removal negotiations in 1831–1832 and settlement in Indian Territory. She describes the 1867 separation of the Eastern Shawnee and Seneca, allotment in 1888, and organization under the 1936 Oklahoma Indian Welfare Act. This is a dated historical outline, not an interpretation of current rights.

Read the sources [1] Oklahoma Historical Society, The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture

02

An educational project directed toward community history

The Tribe’s educator’s companion presents historical recovery as a response to citizens’ requests for learning about culture and arts. Its introduction describes bringing together written sources, language recordings and oral histories. The companion is a public educational work; its linked book, digital collection and recordings are separate materials that were not inspected here.

Read the sources [2] Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma

03

Different experiences within a continuing community

In the companion’s Identity section, chapter synopses discuss cultural autonomy despite shared political arrangements, family discussions of boarding-school experiences, and varied perspectives on Pacific Northwest relocation and reconnection. These are the companion’s summaries of contributing authors’ chapters, rather than findings from the underlying interviews or a rule about Eastern Shawnee identity.

Read the sources [2] Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma

04

A 2024 return visit as education and public history

Adriana Martinez-Smiley’s June 2024 WYSO report follows an Eastern Shawnee educational visit to Ohio. Glenna Wallace explains the importance of learning history before and during return visits; participant Chris Samples discusses the opportunity for Shawnee governments to tell their own stories. Their comments document named people’s perspectives at that time and show history being taught and discussed by a living community.

Read the sources [3] WYSO, republished by WOSU Public Media
